Step 4 · Technical requirements

Translate building conditions into specifications.

These selections become minimum or preferred requirements in the generated RFP. Connectivity and power options are set in the detailed worksheet below.

Performance and deployment baseline

Use these vendor-neutral specifications as a starting point. Confirm every requirement against the district’s objectives, applicable codes, current standards, and the selected sensor technology before solicitation.

Sensor transparencyIdentify sensing technology, manufacturer, model, known interferences, firmware, and substitutions.
Data continuityFive-minute-or-shorter reporting, at least 90% completeness, local buffering, and automatic backfill.
Calibration and QADocument factory records, field verification, automatic correction, recalibration, replacement, and audit trail.
CO₂ evidencePrefer NDIR or equivalent; request range, resolution, accuracy, drift, climate effects, and independent test evidence.
PM₂.₅ evidenceRequest accuracy across typical and smoke-event levels plus humidity, aerosol, coarse-particle, drift, and recovery results.
Representative placementOccupied zone, away from localized sources and supply air; document coverage, exceptions, and post-installation checks.

Help me choose a monitoring type

Compare the operating model, measurements, staffing needs, data capabilities, strengths, and limitations of the three primary monitor types.

Comparison factorHandheld / survey meterPortable / moveable loggerStationary / continuous network
Best fit / questionShort investigations, spot checks, room-to-room screening, complaint response, and verification by trained staff.Temporary monitoring over hours to weeks, classroom pilots, comparing spaces, wildfire-smoke checks, or testing an intervention before scaling.Ongoing room or building oversight, automated alerts, facilities response, public dashboards, or integration with building systems.
Typical measuresOften configurable: CO₂, PM₂.₅/PM₁₀, temperature, and RH; professional units may add CO, VOCs, or specific gases.Commonly CO₂, PM₂.₅, temperature, and RH; some add VOC/NOₓ indices, pressure, location, or outdoor capability.Usually CO₂, PM₂.₅, temperature, and RH; commercial systems may add VOCs, CO, formaldehyde, ozone, NO₂, or other gases.
Setup and staff effortLow installation effort; highest operator effort. Staff need a repeatable sampling plan and must document time, location, occupancy, HVAC status, and outdoor conditions.Place in a representative breathing zone, away from doors, windows, supply diffusers, direct sun, and pollutant sources. Move only on a documented schedule.Moderate-to-high setup. Requires a placement plan, device inventory, network/security review, owners for alerts, maintenance, calibration or field checks, and data retention.
Power and connectivityRechargeable or replaceable batteries. Data are usually viewed on-device and exported by USB or app; cloud connectivity is uncommon.Battery, USB power, or both. Bluetooth and Wi-Fi are common; offline storage varies. Confirm school-network compatibility.Continuous wall or USB power, direct wiring, or PoE; some battery sensors use a hub. Wi-Fi, Ethernet, radio gateways, and cloud services are common.
Data and alertsImmediate readings; many units can log. Alerts and fleet dashboards are usually limited.On-device display and/or app; trend export is common. Some devices offer cloud dashboards, APIs, and alerts.Best option for continuous trends, remote fleet management, alerts, APIs, and dashboards; subscription terms vary.
StrengthsFast and flexible; one device can compare many rooms. Professional instruments can support troubleshooting and calibration workflows.Flexible and easier to pilot than a fixed network; captures trends and supports before/after comparisons.Persistent visibility across time and locations; supports rapid response and evaluation of building operations.
Watch-outsA snapshot can miss changing conditions. Results are sensitive to sampling method and operator practice. Low-cost gas or VOC readings may be only indicative.Moving a logger creates gaps and makes room comparisons harder. Battery charging, clock synchronization, data ownership, and Wi-Fi access need a plan.Greater IT and operational burden. Sensor drift, replacement intervals, subscriptions, cybersecurity, alert fatigue, and vendor lock-in must be managed.

Selection tip: Choose the type that matches the decision and operating model. A district may combine types when ongoing oversight and follow-up investigations are both required. Confirm measurement performance, placement, maintenance, data ownership, network compatibility, and staff responsibilities before procurement.
